claims.text: Increasing the synthesis quench rate increases nanoparticle defect density.
Quench rate establishes the atomic-scale configurational disorder of the nanoparticles.
A higher density of metastable defects increases configurational entropy.
Increased configurational entropy counteracts the thermodynamic drive for elemental segregation.
Defect-mediated configurational entropy delays phase separation and structural degradation during high-temperature exposure.
Cooling or processing conditions can affect composition, chemical ordering, and phase stability in multielement alloys.
Rapidly quenched nanoparticles will exhibit a later onset of phase segregation than slowly quenched nanoparticles.
Rapidly quenched nanoparticles will retain a more homogeneous chemical state at high temperature than slowly quenched nanoparticles.
Nanoparticles made under standard slower-quench conditions have lower defect density.
Lower defect density makes slowly quenched nanoparticles more susceptible to elemental segregation under thermal stress.
Changing only quench rate while holding composition and other processing parameters constant is the proposed controlled intervention.
The proposed catalytic service-temperature range is 773–1173 K.
The proposed thermoelectric service-temperature range is 473–1923 K.
Oxygen partial pressure can strongly affect phase stability and therefore must be controlled when oxidation-sensitive systems are tested.
The proposed stabilization mechanism requires the nanoparticles to retain near-equiatomic composition.
Excessively high quench rates can introduce deleterious thermal stresses.
Excessively high quench rates can cause sintering.
In situ high-temperature X-ray diffraction, TEM, and spatially resolved chemical analysis can jointly compare phase-segregation onset, defect density, and elemental homogeneity.
Failure of rapid quenching to produce both higher defect density and delayed segregation or degradation relative to the slow-quench control is stated to falsify the mechanism.

contradictions.description: The design seeks to attribute changes solely to defect density, but the hypothesis also identifies atomic-scale disorder as a mediator and acknowledges that quench rate can introduce thermal stress or sintering. Varying quench rate therefore does not inherently isolate defect density from these competing quench-induced changes.
